explanations: luna: The section joins remembering with reciting and retaining scripture. This verse asks how people can command righteousness while forgetting themselves even as they recite the Book, bringing reading and failure to remember into one rebuke. | terra: The addressees recite the Book yet “forget yourselves”; the verse exposes a failure to retain and enact the very writing being read.
terra: Israel is told to hold firmly what was given and remember what is in it, directly pairing custody of an entrusted revelation with active remembrance.
terra: People write a book with their own hands and falsely call it from Allah, a direct counterfeit of divinely given words gathered into authentic pages.
terra: Israel is told to hold firmly what it was given and listen, but answers with hearing and disobedience; reception without faithful custody reverses the intended holding.
terra: Gabriel brings the revelation onto the Prophet's heart by Allah's permission while confirming earlier revelation, joining inward retention to continuity across scriptures.
terra: A party given the Book casts Allah's Book behind their backs, turning the section's figurative “dropped” word into an enacted rejection of written revelation.

luna: The section's 87:7 has an exception “except what Allah wills,” and its dictionary defines forgetting as no longer holding what was entrusted. This verse says Allah may cause a verse to be forgotten or replace it, making divine will govern what is retained; here the context is revelation being replaced. | terra: The divine prerogative to abrogate an ayah or cause it to be forgotten marks the explicit boundary around the promise of non-forgetting: any loss is under God's will and replacement.

luna: The section's dictionary form قرأت الشيء defines reading as joining words together. This verse says the people given the Book recite it as it should be recited and believe in it, linking faithful reading with receiving scripture. | terra: Those given the Book recite it with its true recitation, presenting faithful reading as the proper handling of an entrusted scripture.

luna: The section connects the recited word and written scripture with purification. Abraham asks for a messenger who recites God's signs, teaches the Book and wisdom, and purifies the people, bringing those same acts together in one request. | terra: Abraham asks for a messenger who will recite God's signs and teach the Book, anticipating the movement from divinely supplied utterance to learned scripture.

luna: This repeats the prophetic pattern of reciting God's signs, purifying the audience, and teaching the Book. Its own address says the Messenger also teaches what the people did not know, extending the section's meeting of recitation, purification, and scripture to its immediate audience. | terra: The sent messenger recites signs, purifies, and teaches the Book and wisdom, describing the public transmission that follows the Prophet's receipt of recitation.

luna: The section treats remembering as the opposite of forgetting. “فَاذْكُرُونِي أَذْكُرْكُمْ” makes that relation reciprocal, adding what answered remembrance looks like in a direct address to believers.

luna: The section links written pages with a تذكرة that brings a needed matter back to mind. In the debt-writing instructions, witnesses are chosen so that if one errs, “فَتُذَكِّرَ إِحْدَاهُمَا الْأُخْرَى”; writing and mutual reminding protect a detail from being lost. | terra: A second witness is to remind the first if she errs, a concrete legal use of تذكر as retrieving a detail that escaped memory.

luna: After the debt-writing instructions in 2:282, this verse says that when people trust one another without a written pledge, the entrusted party must discharge the trust. Its own contribution is a concrete safeguard against losing what was entrusted.

luna: The section's dictionary distinguishes forgetting through a weak heart, inattention, or intent. This prayer asks not to be taken to task if the believers forget or err, naming ordinary failure of recall as a human limit. | terra: Each soul receives what it earned, and believers pray not to be held accountable if they forget or err; personal share and human forgetting occur together as in the contents of the earlier pages.
terra: A group twists its tongues with the Book so listeners think the utterance belongs to the Book when it does not; oral delivery is severed from its written source.

luna: The section notes how purified pages hold a reminder. This verse joins the Messenger's reciting God's signs, purifying people, and teaching them the Book and wisdom, giving a direct meeting of recitation, purification, and scripture. | terra: The messenger recites signs and teaches the Book to a people formerly astray, repeating the prophetic chain from received words to taught writing.
terra: Those charged to disclose the Book cast it behind their backs and trade it away, showing entrusted writing deliberately abandoned rather than retained and transmitted.

luna: The section's dictionary defines forgetting as failing to keep what was entrusted. This verse commands that trusts be returned to their rightful owners, stating the affirmative counterpart to letting an entrusted thing go.
terra: A portion of what the covenant people were reminded of was forgotten; this is precisely an entrusted divine communication no longer held intact.
terra: Those who claimed Christianity likewise forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of, a repeated scriptural instance of loss from entrusted memory.
terra: After 5:13-14's forgotten portions, the Messenger exposes much that the People of the Book had hidden; it suggests recovery into disclosure, though concealment is not identical to forgetting.

luna: The section describes prophetic books as reminders that are held in written pages. This verse says the rabbis and scholars were entrusted with God's Book and charged to preserve it, making custodianship of revealed scripture explicit. | terra: The rabbis and scholars judge by the Torah because they were entrusted with preserving Allah's Book; this states the section's image of written revelation deposited for human custody.
terra: Jesus follows earlier prophets with the Gospel, confirming the Torah and providing guidance and admonition, showing revelation retained and relayed across successive books.

luna: The section says the Quran's message is also present in earlier prophetic books. This verse describes the Quran as confirming the earlier Scripture and overseeing it, specifying the relation between the present recitation and prior revelation. | terra: The present Book comes in truth, confirming prior scripture and serving as its guardian; the verse defines continuity and custody across the gathered prophetic writings.

luna: The section's suhuf are pieces bearing writing. This verse imagines a Book sent down on parchment that people touch with their hands, then records their response that it is manifest magic; the physical page does not guarantee acceptance of its message. | terra: Even a Book sent down on قِرْطَاس and touched by their hands would be dismissed as magic; the physical sheet clarifies that material presence alone does not secure reception.

luna: The section links admonition to remembrance. Here, after people forget what they were reminded of, they are given what they seek before sudden punishment comes; the verse shows what refusal of the reminder permits. | terra: When a people forget what they were reminded of, their apparent abundance becomes the prelude to sudden seizure; the specific link is reminder received and then lost.

luna: The section joins what falls away with what is held and written. This verse says that not even a leaf falls without God's knowledge, and that what is moist or dry is in a clear book; the falling object and the preserved record meet in one ayah. | terra: No leaf falls without Allah knowing it, nothing hidden escapes Him, and all is in a clear Book; falling, hiddenness, knowledge, and written retention meet in one verse.
terra: If Satan makes the Prophet forget the command to leave mockers, he is to act after recollection; this supplies a bounded, recoverable forgetting alongside 87:6-7's promise.

luna: The section describes written pages gathered as scripture. This verse speaks of making the Book into sheets, then “يُبْدُونَهَا وَيُخْفُونَ كَثِيرًا”; it adds the boundary between what is exposed and what is hidden in a written revelation. | terra: Moses' Book is turned into قَرَاطِيس that people display in part and hide in part; this directly stages earlier revelation as separate written sheets subject to human concealment.
terra: The present blessed Book confirms what came before it, completing 6:91's scene of Mosaic sheets with continuity rather than concealment.

luna: The section's dictionary form النسي means inferior belongings left at the stations of departing travelers. Here people stand before God having “تَرَكْتُمْ مَا خَوَّلْنَاكُمْ وَرَاءَ ظُهُورِكُمْ”; the verse stages people leaving their worldly goods behind when they arrive.

luna: The section quotes the teaching of Ibrahim and Moses' pages that no burden-bearer carries another's burden. This verse repeats that rule while saying each soul's gain is its own and all return to God. | terra: No bearer bears another's burden and every soul earns only against itself, repeating the first teaching quoted from the pages in 53:38.

luna: The section's dictionary form النسيان includes leaving something behind. This verse says those deceived by worldly life forgot the meeting of that day, and today they are forgotten; it connects deliberate neglect to the passage's contrast of what lasts and what passes. | terra: Those deceived by the worldly life forgot the meeting of their Day, so they are “forgotten”; the verse joins worldly preference to reciprocal abandonment.

luna: The section names Moses' pages and defines a reminder as what recalls a needed matter. This verse says God wrote admonition and detailed instruction for Moses on the tablets, giving a concrete written source of reminder. | terra: Allah writes admonition and detailed instruction for Moses on the tablets, then tells him to take them firmly; writing, reminder, and active holding coincide.

luna: This continues Moses' tablets after he takes them up again: their inscription contains guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord. It adds the content and audience of the written reminder. | terra: When Moses takes up the tablets, their inscription contains guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord, joining written custody to the fearing recipient of reminder.
terra: The unlettered Messenger is found described in the Torah and Gospel, a specific instance of present prophetic reality preserved in earlier writings.
terra: Those who forget what they were reminded of are separated from those who prohibited evil, making retained warning the line between two outcomes.

luna: The section connects the first pages with the choice to prefer worldly life. This verse describes heirs of the Book taking the fleeting world's goods, though they studied its contents; it then says the Hereafter is better, bringing scripture reception and worldly preference together in one scene.

luna: This follows 7:169's heirs who take worldly gain despite their Book by praising those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer. It supplies the contrasting response of keeping the scripture's instruction.
terra: The command خُذُوا مَا آتَيْنَاكُم بِقُوَّةٍ وَاذْكُرُوا مَا فِيهِ again makes holding the Book and remembering its contents one act.
luna: The section says the one who fears will remember. This verse likewise places fear before recovery of attention: when the God-fearing are touched by Satan, they remember and see clearly.

luna: The section's image asks how a recited word is gathered and retained. This verse says to listen and be quiet when the Quran is recited, giving the hearer's attentive reception as a counterpart to the Prophet's paced recitation.

luna: The section says people prefer the nearer life although the Hereafter is better and more lasting. This verse directly asks whether they are content with worldly life over the Hereafter, then calls worldly enjoyment small beside it.

luna: The section itself cites “نَسُوا اللَّهَ فَنَسِيَهُمْ.” In context this describes hypocrites who command wrong and withhold good; Allah's answering “forgetting” is the reversal of their deliberate abandonment. | terra: نَسُوا اللَّهَ فَنَسِيَهُمْ explicitly turns human forgetting of God into God's abandonment of them, the very secondary sense used in the source section.

luna: The section's dictionary form النسي names what falls away after departure. This verse stages earth's vegetation flourishing, then becoming “حَصِيدًا” as though it had not flourished the day before, an explicit image of what passes and is left behind.
terra: The verse moves from the Prophet reciting Quran to God's witnessing and a clear Book from which no particle is absent, specifically connecting recitation with exhaustive record.
terra: Those who read the Book before the Prophet are named as witnesses to prior revelation, linking present recitation with an older community of readers.

luna: The section's dictionary form النسيان includes losing hold of what one should remember. On the usual reading that the released prisoner forgot Joseph's request to mention him to the ruler, the verse shows a lost reminder prolonging Joseph's imprisonment; the referent of “his lord” is also read differently. | terra: Satan makes the released prisoner forget to mention Joseph to his lord; a needed report is not transmitted because it drops from memory.
terra: The man who forgot Joseph in 12:42 remembers after a long interval and offers to transmit the needed interpretation; this completes forgetting with recovery and report.

luna: The section explicitly sets forgetting against حفظ, keeping or guarding what was entrusted. Joseph offers himself as “حَفِيظٌ عَلِيمٌ” over the storehouses, giving a concrete instance of guarding an entrusted provision, though here the object is grain rather than remembered revelation.

luna: The section's exception places retention under Allah's will. This verse says Allah erases what He wills and confirms what He wills, with the source-record with Him; it gives a written-decree parallel while speaking of decree rather than human memory.
terra: Those who prefer worldly life over the Hereafter are identified by that preference, directly restating the stance criticized at 87:16.
terra: A good word is compared to a good tree with a firm root and high branches, giving a nonlexical image of speech that is held rather than dropped.
terra: The good word's tree continually gives fruit by its Lord's permission, showing what a firmly retained word goes on producing.
terra: A corrupt word is like a tree uprooted from the earth with no stability, a precise reversal of the section's gathered and securely held word.
terra: Allah makes believers firm through the firm word in this life and the Hereafter, naming divine stabilization as the reason the word does not fall away.

luna: The section's dictionary form النسيان is the opposite of remembering and preserving. Allah calls the revelation “الذِّكْرَ” and says He guards it, joining reminder to preservation directly. | terra: Allah says He sent down الذِّكْر and will guard it; the verse unites revelation as Reminder with the divine preservation promised by “you will not forget.”
terra: “Ask the people of the Reminder” treats custodians of prior revelation as people defined by the retained prophetic book, though the written medium is implicit.
terra: Earlier messengers came with proofs and زُبُر, while the Reminder is sent to the Prophet for explanation; written predecessors and present dhikr are placed in one transmission chain.

luna: The section's dictionary describes forgetting as letting something go and its final contrast names what remains. This verse says “مَا عِنْدَكُمْ يَنْفَدُ وَمَا عِنْدَ اللَّهِ بَاقٍ,” sharply stating what passes and what endures. | terra: What people possess runs out while what is with Allah remains, stating the passing-versus-retained relation that the section makes perceptible through memory and pages.

luna: The section's dictionary form تُؤْثِرُونَ means preferring one thing to another. This verse says the people “اسْتَحَبُّوا الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا عَلَى الْآخِرَةِ,” making the same preference explicit in its own account of those who reject faith. | terra: Disbelief is explained by preferring worldly life over the Hereafter, another explicit boundary between the passing and enduring objects of choice.

luna: The section's image moves from what is held in memory to what is written and gathered on pages. This verse says each person's record is attached to them and brought out as an open book, transferring the image of retained writing to an individual's deeds. | terra: Each person's record is brought out as a كتاب مَّنشُور at resurrection, giving a concrete scene of previously gathered material opened for reading.

luna: The section's dictionary form قرأت الشيء defines reading as gathering words together, and its pages are written records. Here the person is told “اقْرَأْ كِتَابَكَ,” to read their own open record, making the act of reading answerable to what was retained. | terra: “Read your book” transfers the root قرأ to a person's fully gathered record, showing reading as taking together the written account that confronts its owner.

luna: The section quotes the first pages' rule that no burden-bearer carries another's burden. This verse repeats it and adds that God does not punish until sending a messenger, connecting individual responsibility with the reminder carried by revelation. | terra: No burdened soul bears another's burden, independently repeating the teaching preserved in the Mosaic and Abrahamic pages.

luna: The section contrasts preferring near life with the better Hereafter. This verse describes one who desires “الْعَاجِلَةَ” and the limited worldly provision granted, giving the immediate-life choice its own consequence.

luna: This follows the desire for the immediate in 17:18 with the person who desires the Hereafter and strives for it. It adds the positive counter-choice to the section's preference/lasting contrast.

luna: The section concerns recited revelation and the audience that turns from its reminder. This verse says a hidden barrier is placed between the Prophet and those who do not believe in the Hereafter when he recites the Quran, making refusal a response to the very act of recitation.

luna: This continues 17:45 by describing veils over their hearts and heaviness in their ears when the Prophet recites the Quran. Its contribution is the impaired reception that completes the barrier image.
terra: Allah could, if He willed, take away what He revealed to the Prophet; this identifies the divine-will boundary behind the continued presence of the recited deposit.
terra: The skeptics demand that a book descend for them to read, a physicalized demand for revelation comparable to the opened pages demanded in 74:52.

luna: The section's dictionary form قرأت الشيء means gathering parts together. Here the Quran is divided for people to be recited “عَلَى مُكْثٍ,” linking collected revelation to its gradual public reading. | terra: The Quran is divided so the Prophet may recite it to people deliberately, and it is sent down in stages; collected reading is delivered in an ordered temporal form.

luna: The section itself cites the instruction “وَاذْكُر رَّبَّكَ إِذَا نَسِيتَ.” It supplies the remedy for the very failure named by its dictionary: when you forget, remember your Lord. | terra: The exception “unless Allah wills” is followed by وَاذْكُر رَبَّكَ إِذَا نَسِيتَ; it joins divine willing, forgetting, and remembrance as the recovery from forgetting.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to recite the revealed Book, whose words none can change; oral delivery is anchored in an inviolable divine text.

luna: The section's dictionary links forgetting with letting go of remembrance, and 87:16 names preference for worldly life. This verse describes a person whose heart is heedless of God's remembrance, who follows desire; it joins lost remembrance to the desire that the section contrasts with the lasting Hereafter.

luna: The section's dictionary form النسي is fallen debris left after departure. This parable says the rain-grown vegetation becomes “هَشِيمًا تَذْرُوهُ الرِّيَاحُ,” plant fragments scattered by wind; the object that was flourishing becomes what is dispersed.

luna: The section contrasts the alluring nearer life with what lasts. This verse calls wealth and children an adornment of worldly life, then says abiding good works are better with the Lord in reward and hope.

luna: The section describes a mushaf as a gathering of written pages. Here the placed record leaves no small or great deed uncounted, and people find what they did present; it gives a specific picture of a record that does not drop what it holds. | terra: The judgment Book leaves no small or great deed unenumerated; its exhaustive gathering illuminates the image of nothing entrusted being dropped.

luna: The section's reminder is something that brings a need back to mind. Here the wrongdoer is reminded of the Lord's signs, turns away, and forgets what his hands sent ahead; remembrance and deliberate neglect are placed in one scene. | terra: One reminded of the Lord's signs turns away and forgets what his hands sent ahead; remembrance offered and morally consequential forgetting are directly opposed.
terra: Two travelers forget their fish at the meeting place and it departs into the sea, an unusually exact Quranic scene for the dictionary image of an item left at a travelers' stopping place.

luna: The section's dictionary form النسيان includes failing to retain what was entrusted. Here Moses' companion says he forgot the fish and that Satan made him forget to mention it, a concrete lapse about something carried on their journey. | terra: At the rock, the servant recalls that he forgot the fish and even forgot to mention it; a lost object and a lost report are recovered together through recollection.
terra: They turn back عَلَىٰ آثَارِهِمَا, retracing their tracks to seek what escaped; this enacts the section's definition of recollection as “seeking what has gone.”

luna: The section's dictionary describes forgetting as failing to keep something in mind. Moses says “لَا تُؤَاخِذْنِي بِمَا نَسِيتُ,” acknowledging a lapse in their exchange and asking pardon. | terra: Moses asks not to be blamed for forgetting his undertaking, another narrative case of a condition entrusted to a person but not held; its tie is to ordinary human failure rather than revelation.
terra: If the sea were ink for the Lord's words, the sea would run out before those words did; material inscription cannot exhaust the speech it tries to gather.

luna: The section's dictionary form النسي names forgotten or abandoned things as well as the failure to remember. Maryam wishes she had become “نَسْيًا مَّنْسِيًّا,” a thing forgotten; this related form shifts from the section's dropped belongings to a person wishing to disappear from memory.

luna: The section's dictionary form النسيان is what is opposite to remembrance and keeping. In its own context the angels say, “وَمَا كَانَ رَبُّكَ نَسِيًّا,” a compact parallel to the Lord who does not forget in 20:52.
terra: Allah makes the revelation easy on the Prophet's tongue for glad tidings and warning, a vocal counterpart to the promise of facilitated recitation.
terra: Moses and Aaron are told to address Pharaoh gently so that he may remember or fear; it pairs تذكّر and خشية just as 87:9-10 does.

luna: Pharaoh asks Moses about “الْقُرُونِ الْأُولَى,” the earlier generations. The section's dictionary form الأُولى means the beginning or earliest part; Moses' answer in 20:52 then connects those generations with a book held by God. | terra: Pharaoh's question about the القُرُونِ الأُولَى, former generations, supplies the “first/former” side of the answer in 20:52, where their knowledge is retained in writing.

luna: The section itself cites Moses' answer: their knowledge is with his Lord in a book, and his Lord neither strays nor forgets. This directly joins a written record of the earlier generations to divine non-forgetting. | terra: The former generations' knowledge is in a كتاب, and Moses says his Lord neither goes astray nor يَنسَى; writing and the unfailing divine memory coincide exactly as in the section.
terra: The magicians refuse to prefer Pharaoh over the clear signs that came to them; their use of نُّؤْثِرَ is the moral reverse of preferring the nearer life over enduring revelation.

luna: The section's dictionary form أَثَرْتُ الحديث means transmitting another's speech. Moses' rebuke instead uses “أَثَرِ الرَّسُولِ” for a trace of the messenger: the related root shifts from transmitted words to a remaining trace, making the difference between report and residue visible. | terra: The Samiri takes a handful from أَثَرِ الرَّسُول and casts it away; a messenger's trace is physically gathered and then dropped, a pointed reversal of the held transmitted word.
terra: Allah relates reports of what has gone before and gives the Prophet a Reminder from Himself, joining transmitted earlier narrative to a present prophetic book.

luna: The section itself cites this command to the Prophet not to hurry with the Quran before its revelation is completed. It joins the Quran's arrival to the section's promise of recitation and retention. | terra: The Prophet is told not to hurry the Quran before its revelation is completed; like 87:6, the verse makes reception depend on God's completed delivery rather than anxious self-retention.

luna: The section itself identifies Adam's forgotten charge as the first example of human forgetting. The ayah says he forgot the covenant and lacked resolve, giving a concrete instance of failing to hold what had been entrusted. | terra: Adam forgets a covenant previously entrusted to him, a direct narrative instance of نسي as failing to hold what was deposited with a person.

luna: The section's dictionary form النسيان is paired with remembrance and the admonition in 87:9. Here turning away from Allah's remembrance brings a constricted life, showing a consequence of abandoning that reminder. | terra: Turning away from Allah's Reminder leads to a constricted life and blindness at resurrection, establishing the rejected reminder whose forgotten signs are named in 20:126.
terra: The raised person asks why he is blind although he once saw; this question lets 20:126 explain that forgotten signs yield a corresponding abandonment.

luna: The section itself quotes this reversal: people forgot Allah's signs when they came, and on that day they are forgotten. It gives the abandonment-and-return pattern in the dictionary and 87:7 a judgment scene. | terra: A person who forgot the arriving signs is in turn “forgotten”; the reciprocal wording realizes the section's secondary sense of forgetting as deliberate abandonment.

luna: The section itself cites the question whether the people have received proof of what is in the earlier pages. This ayah directly connects the dictionary's “earliest” pages with evidence presented to an audience. | terra: The “clear proof” is explicitly connected with what is in الصُّحُفِ الأُولَى, another direct witness that guidance now delivered was already held in the first pages.
terra: The repeated command to ask the people of the Reminder again identifies earlier scriptural knowledge with a community that preserves and can transmit it.
terra: Allah has sent down a كتاب containing the addressees' ذِكْر, explicitly placing remembrance within a revealed book.
terra: “This is the Reminder of those with me and those before me” places present and earlier communities' revelation under the single category of dhikr.
terra: Moses and Aaron receive the Criterion, illumination, and a Reminder for the God-fearing, identifying Mosaic revelation with the same dhikr-function as the pages in 87:19.

luna: The section's dictionary says that the books of the prophets are ذكر. This verse calls the revelation “ذِكْرٌ مُّبَارَكٌ” and says it was sent down, directly joining a prophetic book to the section's reminder sense. | terra: The present revelation is a blessed Reminder sent down, continuing the prophetic-book sense of ذكر without naming its written form.
luna: The section describes sheets gathered in a book. This verse likens the rolling up of the sky to the rolling of a written scroll, extending the page image to a record being closed at the end.
terra: Allah says He wrote in the Zabur after the Reminder; the verse links divine writing and prior scripture, though “the Reminder” may denote a heavenly record or an earlier revelation.

luna: The section's dictionary form الذكر is both remembrance and the reminder that restores it. This verse says mockery of the believers led the mockers to forget Allah's remembrance, showing how rejection of the reminder can invert the relation. | terra: Mockery of the believers makes the rejecters forget Allah's remembrance, showing attention displaced until the reminder is no longer held.

luna: The section says Allah gathers and has the Prophet recite revelation, while a dictionary branch names speech transmitted from another. Here opponents allege that the Quran is old tales written down and dictated to the Prophet; the ayah supplies a specific human-copying counterclaim to the section's account of divinely given recitation. | terra: The hostile claim says the Quran is tales of the former peoples that the Prophet had written down and that are dictated to him; it is a precise counterfeit of the section's divine gathering, recitation, and earlier pages.
terra: The answer to 25:5 says the One who knows the secret in heaven and earth sent it down, restoring divine authorship and hidden knowledge against the scribal accusation.
terra: Long enjoyment causes a people to forget الذِّكْر, concretely linking preference for passing worldly provision with loss of the enduring reminder.
terra: A companion leads the speaker away from the Reminder after it came to him; the verse stages received guidance being abandoned rather than held.

luna: The section's dictionary form النسيان includes leaving something behind. Here the Messenger complains that his people have taken the Quran as “مَهْجُورًا,” abandoned; it makes neglect of the revealed word explicit.

luna: The objection asks why the Quran was not sent down all at once; the answer says it was sent thus to strengthen the Prophet's heart and recited in order. That adds why a gathered, paced revelation supports retention. | terra: The Quran's staged descent strengthens the Prophet's heart and Allah says وَرَتَّلْنَاهُ تَرْتِيلًا; measured joining in recitation serves inward retention.
terra: The passage begins by identifying the Quran as a sending-down from the Lord of the worlds, establishing the divine source of the word later said to be in former books.
terra: The trustworthy Spirit brings the revelation down, making the transmission to the Prophet an entrusted delivery rather than a human compilation.
terra: The revelation descends عَلَىٰ قَلْبِكَ, placing the transmitted words in the heart that must hold them so the Prophet can warn.
terra: The delivered revelation is in a clear Arabic tongue, completing the move from divine descent to articulated, recitable words.

luna: The section itself cites “وَإِنَّهُ لَفِي زُبُرِ الْأَوَّلِينَ.” Its claim that the Quran is in the books of earlier peoples joins the recited revelation to the section's dictionary sense of the first writings. | terra: The Quran is said to be in زُبُرِ الأَوَّلِينَ, directly paralleling the section's claim that the recited word is also gathered in earlier scriptures.
terra: Knowledge of the Quran among the scholars of Israel serves as a living sign of the attestation in former books stated in 26:196.
terra: Nothing hidden in heaven or earth is absent from a clear Book, joining hiddenness to written divine retention as 87:7 joins it to divine knowledge.
terra: After the former generations, Allah gives Moses the Book as insight, guidance, and mercy so that people may remember; earlier time, Mosaic writing, and recollection meet explicitly.

luna: The section's 87:16–17 contrasts worldly life with what is better and enduring. This verse sets the world's enjoyment and adornment against what is with God, “خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ,” an especially close formulation of that contrast. | terra: Worldly possessions are passing enjoyment and adornment, while what is with Allah is better and more enduring; the wording closely parallels the choice in 87:16-17.
terra: “Do not forget your share of the world” sets a boundary around the dunya/Hereafter contrast: worldly participation is retained without making the nearer life the preferred end.

luna: The section joins recitation, remembrance, and prayer through the surah's named roots. This verse commands reciting the Book and establishing prayer, then says remembrance of God is greater, bringing those acts together and adding prayer's effect in its context.

luna: The section links recitation with written pages and earlier scripture. This verse says the Prophet had not recited a book before the Quran or written one with his hand; its own contribution is to distinguish his prior state from the revelation whose pages the section describes. | terra: Before the Quran the Prophet neither recited a book nor wrote one with his right hand; the verse sharply distinguishes oral reception from human inscription while 29:49 locates the signs inwardly.

terra: In contrast to the absent prior reading or handwriting in 29:48, the revelation is clear signs in the breasts of those given knowledge, an inward repository rather than the Prophet's authored page.
terra: Even all trees as pens and seas as ink would not exhaust Allah's words, setting a limit on pages while affirming the inexhaustibility of divine speech.

luna: The section's dictionary form النسيان is the opposite of preserving in memory. Here the people are told they are forgotten because they forgot the meeting of this day, repeating the reciprocal reversal in a distinct judgment address. | terra: Because they forgot the meeting of the Day, they are told “We have forgotten you,” a direct reversal from failed human remembrance to divine abandonment.
terra: The Prophet's wives are told to remember what is recited in their houses of Allah's signs and wisdom, directly linking oral recital with deliberate retention.

luna: The section quotes the earlier pages' rule that no burden-bearer carries another's burden. This verse repeats it and says even a heavily burdened soul cannot have its load carried by another, clarifying the rule's force. | terra: No burdened soul can carry another's burden, even when a heavily laden person calls for help; the ayah expands the earlier pages' teaching with a concrete boundary.

luna: The section connects fear with remembering: “سَيَذَّكَّرُ مَنْ يَخْشَىٰ.” This verse similarly says the warning benefits one who follows the Reminder and fears the Merciful, linking the audience's fear to response. | terra: The effective warning reaches one who follows the Reminder and fears the Merciful unseen, again binding reception of remembrance to fear.

luna: The section's dictionary form أَثَرَ الحديث names something transmitted, while its نسي entry names what is left behind. This verse says God records what people send ahead and “آثَارَهُمْ,” the traces they leave, joining remembered transmission to written record. | terra: Allah writes what people sent ahead and their آثَار, then enumerates all things in a clear register; “traces” and exhaustive written preservation meet in the root family noted by the section.
terra: The revelation is “only a Reminder and a clear Quran,” placing ذكر and قرآن side by side as two aspects of the same delivered speech.

terra: The skeptic “forgets his creation”; this may illuminate forgetting one's beginning, which the section associates with الأوّل, but the verse concerns resurrection rather than preservation of words.
terra: The oath by “the Quran possessed of Reminder” joins recited text and الذكر in one compact description, though it does not itself describe the act of preservation.

luna: The section quotes the pages' rule that no burden-bearer carries another's burden. This verse repeats it and says people will be informed of their deeds when they return to God, joining individual responsibility to a final record. | terra: No bearer bears another's burden, again preserving across the Quran the teaching identified as content of the first pages.
luna: The section's dictionary form النسي names fallen remnants. Here crops turn yellow and become “حُطَامًا,” giving the brief life of green growth a close image of what remains after it has passed.
terra: Allah sends the best discourse as a harmonious, repeated Book; bodies react and hearts soften to Allah's remembrance, joining articulated text, repetition, and received dhikr.
terra: The worldly life is only temporary enjoyment while the Hereafter is the lasting abode, a direct thematic restatement of the preference boundary.

luna: The section names Moses among the holders of the earlier pages. This verse says God gave Moses guidance and caused the Israelites to inherit the Book, directly extending the transmission of Moses' scripture to a later community.

luna: This completes 40:53 by calling that inherited Book guidance and a reminder for people of understanding. It directly joins Moses' scripture to the section's dictionary sense of prophetic books as remembrance.

luna: The section describes words recited and gathered for the listener. This verse reports disbelievers saying, “لَا تَسْمَعُوا لِهَذَا الْقُرْآنِ,” directly staging refusal to listen to the recitation.

luna: The section links the reminder to written pages and a collected book. This verse calls the Reminder a mighty Book when it comes to people, explicitly joining those two forms of revelation. | terra: The arriving الذِّكْر is immediately identified as a mighty كتاب, explicitly realizing the dictionary sense of Reminder as prophetic book.

luna: This continues the mighty Book in 41:41 by saying falsehood cannot approach it from before or behind. It adds a claim of protection to the section's image of a word preserved in pages. | terra: Falsehood cannot reach the Book from before or behind; this gives the mighty Reminder of 41:41 a textual inviolability corresponding to divinely secured retention.

luna: The section says the Hereafter is better and more lasting than the nearer life. This verse likewise calls what people are given in worldly life enjoyment and says what is with God is “خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ.” | terra: What people receive is enjoyment of worldly life, whereas what is with Allah is better and more enduring for believers, another direct formulation of the section's value contrast.
terra: Allah makes the revelation an Arabic Quran so people may understand, supplying the articulated recitation whose written heavenly locus is named in 43:4.
terra: The revelation is in أُمِّ الْكِتَابِ with Allah, exalted and wise; it provides a heavenly written locus for the recited message.

luna: The section's dictionary form أَثَرْتُ الحديث describes transmitting a saying from someone else. This verse says the polytheists found their fathers following a way and follow “آثَارِهِمْ”; here the related root is ancestral tracks, contrasting inherited custom with the earlier prophetic pages the section names.

luna: The section's dictionary form الذكر includes a book containing the religion's details. This verse calls the revelation a reminder for the Prophet and his people and says they will be questioned about it, connecting scripture with an address that is retained and answered. | terra: The Quran is a ذِكْر for the Prophet and his people and they will be questioned about it, treating the revelation as a retained charge as well as remembrance.
terra: Allah says the revelation was made easy “in your tongue” so that they may remember, bringing vocal delivery, ease, and recollection into one formulation.
terra: Every community is summoned to its Book for judgment, setting the scene for the divinely copied record that speaks in 45:29.
terra: Allah's Book speaks truth because human deeds were being copied into it, another concrete mechanism by which what passes is retained in writing.

luna: The section's dictionary form النسيان includes leaving behind. Here those who mocked the meeting of this day are told they will be forgotten as they forgot it, a second explicit reversal of the memory relation. | terra: The condemned are forgotten as they forgot the meeting of their Day, repeating the deliberate-leaving sense of نسي as retribution.

luna: The section's dictionary form أَثَرْتُ الحديث means transmitting a saying from another. This verse asks for an earlier book or “أَثَارَةٍ مِّنْ عِلْمٍ”; the latter is a remnant of knowledge, connecting transmitted words to a trace of earlier teaching. | terra: The challenge asks for an earlier كتاب or an أَثَارَةٍ مِّنْ عِلْمٍ; prior writing and a transmitted remnant of knowledge meet in the root family the section connects with reported speech.
terra: Some listen to the Prophet but immediately ask what he just said after leaving; this is a concrete, nonlexical failure to hold received speech.
terra: The believers bear an أَثَر of prostration on their faces and have corresponding portrayals in the Torah and Gospel; visible trace and earlier scriptural witness meet in one ayah.

luna: The section moves from what is left behind to what is preserved in a record. This verse says God knows what the earth diminishes from the dead and that with Him is a preserving book, joining disappearance with a record that keeps account. | terra: What the earth diminishes from human bodies is known, and with Allah is a حَفِيظ Book; passing material is retained in a preserving record.
terra: No word is uttered without a ready observer, so passing speech is not allowed simply to fall away but is held for record.

luna: The section's dictionary form التذكرة is what restores something to mind. This verse calls the account a reminder for whoever has a heart or gives ear while attentive, explicitly linking reminder to receptive hearing.

luna: The section's 87:9 commands the Prophet to remind, and 87:10 identifies the one who fears as remembering. This verse tells the Prophet to remind by the Quran those who fear its warning, while clarifying that he is not their controller. | terra: فَذَكِّرْ بِالْقُرْآنِ مَن يَخَافُ وَعِيدِ closely repeats the command to remind and identifies the receptive hearer as the one who fears.

luna: The section's dictionary form التذكرة is that by which a need is recalled. This verse commands “وَذَكِّرْ” because reminding benefits believers, directly stating the use of the section's reminder. | terra: The command to remind is justified because الذِّكْرَى benefits believers, a direct parallel to 87:9's condition that the reminder be beneficial.

luna: The section defines a sahifa as a written piece of leather or parchment. The oath “وَكِتَابٍ مَسْطُورٍ فِي رَقٍّ مَنْشُورٍ” explicitly places writing on spread parchment, a material parallel to the section's pages. | terra: The oath by a “Book inscribed” makes writing itself the object of attention, anticipating the material named in the next verse.
terra: The inscribed Book is on رَقٍّ مَّنشُور, an unrolled parchment, matching the section's lexical definition of a sahifa as material written upon.
terra: The Hereafter and الأُولَى both belong to Allah, placing the “first” life and the later life under one ownership beside this surah's earlier-page passage.

luna: The section says the earlier pages contain the message and quotes this opening question about what is in Moses' pages. This verse directly names those pages as the source of the teachings that follow. | terra: The verse asks whether one was informed of what is in صُحُفِ مُوسَى, directly opening the contents of the Mosaic pages named at 87:19.

luna: The section identifies the earlier pages with Ibrahim and Moses. This verse names Ibrahim and says he fulfilled his charge, beginning the specific contents of the pages introduced in 53:36. | terra: Abraham, “the one who fulfilled,” completes the pair of page-bearers named at 87:19 and identifies the second body of earlier scripture whose contents follow.

luna: The section cites the first teaching from the pages: no burden-bearer bears another's burden. This verse is that teaching, giving the remembered scripture a rule of individual responsibility. | terra: The first stated teaching of those pages is that no bearer carries another's burden, making the enduring written reminder assign each person an undropped share.

luna: The section cites the pages' statement that a person has only what they strive for. This verse supplies that specific teaching and links the written reminder to each person's own effort. | terra: The pages say that a human being has only what he strives for; this specifies the individual portion preserved in the earlier record.

luna: This continues the pages' account of individual effort in 53:39: “وَأَنَّ سَعْيَهُ سَوْفَ يُرَىٰ.” Its contribution is that one's effort will be seen, completing what the preceding verse says belongs to a person. | terra: A person's striving will be seen, so the individual share named in 53:39 is not lost from view before recompense.

luna: This continues 53:40 by saying that the effort is then fully recompensed. It adds the outcome of the pages' teaching about each person's own striving. | terra: The striving preserved and shown in 53:39-40 receives its full recompense; this continues the contents of the earlier pages rather than merely standing beside them.

luna: The section quotes the pages' conclusion, “وَأَنَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ الْمُنْتَهَىٰ.” This closes their sequence about individual burden and effort with its destination, rather than leaving the pages as detached maxims. | terra: The sequence of teachings from the Mosaic and Abrahamic pages ends by locating the final destination with the Lord, giving the retained teaching its terminus.

luna: The section's 87:9–10 distinguishes reminder from the one who remembers. This repeated refrain says the Quran was made easy for remembrance and asks whether anyone will remember, connecting recitation's ease to response. | terra: Allah has made the Quran easy for remembrance and asks whether anyone will remember, joining divine facilitation, Quran, and recollection.

luna: This repeats the Quran's being made easy for remembrance, directly joining recited revelation and recall as the section does. | terra: The repeated declaration that the Quran is made easy for remembrance reinforces that ease belongs to the divine handling of the recited text.

luna: This is another occurrence of the refrain that the Quran is made easy for remembrance, showing the repeated invitation to recall the revelation. | terra: A third occurrence preserves the same Quran-remembrance formula, making its recurrence itself part of the text's mnemonic design.

luna: This final occurrence repeats that the Quran is made easy for remembrance, reinforcing the relation between recitation and remembered admonition. | terra: The fourth occurrence completes the repeated refrain that the Quran has been made easy for remembrance and awaits a remembering hearer.
terra: Everything the wrongdoers did is in the زُبُر, using the scripture/record noun for gathered deeds rather than prophetic books.
terra: Every small and great thing is inscribed, explaining the completeness of the records named in 54:52.
terra: عَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ gives Allah the direct role of teaching the Quran, a close counterpart to the causative “We shall make you recite.”
terra: After teaching the Quran in 55:2, Allah teaches the human being clear expression, completing the move from received revelation to articulated speech.
luna: The section contrasts the nearer life with what endures. “كُلُّ مَنْ عَلَيْهَا فَانٍ” states the passing side of that boundary for all on earth.

luna: This continues 55:26's passing of everything on earth with the enduring face of the Lord. Its contribution is the lasting counterpart, clarifying the boundary that 87:17 draws for the Hereafter.
terra: The hearers know the first creation yet are asked why they do not remember; الأُولَى and تَذَكَّرُونَ join beginning with recollection.

luna: The section connects recitation and memory to a written scripture. This verse calls the Quran “كَرِيمٌ,” introducing the revelation described in the following ayat as a noble Quran. | terra: The passage first identifies its object as a noble Quran, keeping recitation before the protected written setting of the next verse.

luna: The section says a mushaf gathers written pages into a book. Here the Quran is “فِي كِتَابٍ مَكْنُونٍ,” explicitly joining recited revelation to a kept book. | terra: The noble Quran is “in a guarded/hidden Book,” giving recited revelation a protected written locus; the precise referent is heavenly rather than an ordinary codex.

luna: This follows the hidden book of 56:78 with a statement about who may touch it. It adds a boundary around access to the written record, which the section's page-and-book image leaves implicit. | terra: The guarded Book is approached only by the purified, linking written revelation with purity as 80:13-14 does, though the nature of the touching is interpretively disputed.

luna: This completes the description in 56:77–79 by calling the Quran a sending-down from the Lord of the worlds. Its contribution identifies the source of the book whose preservation and handling the preceding ayat describe. | terra: The passage closes by naming the Quran as a sending-down from the Lord of the worlds, completing the route from divine source to protected Book.

terra: Believers are summoned to let their hearts respond to the Reminder and truth, unlike earlier recipients of the Book whose hearts hardened over time; it stages retention and loss across scriptural history.

luna: The section's dictionary form النسي names discarded remnants, while 87:16–17 contrasts near life with what lasts. This verse likens worldly growth to rain-fed vegetation that withers into “حُطَامًا,” joining transient adornment to the section's image of fallen remains.
terra: Messengers are sent “upon their traces,” and Jesus is given the Gospel; prophetic succession makes following آثار a vehicle of scriptural transmission.
terra: Allah has enumerated all their deeds while they forgot them (أَحْصَاهُ اللَّهُ وَنَسُوهُ); divine collection preserves exactly what human memory drops.
terra: Satan causes people to forget the remembrance of Allah, making forgetfulness an active displacement of what should occupy and guard memory.

luna: The section's dictionary form تُؤْثِرُونَ means giving one thing preference, and it criticizes preferring the nearer life. This verse uses the same root for the opposite choice: the helpers prefer others over themselves even when needy, showing a reversal in what is given priority.

luna: The section itself cites the warning against people who forget Allah and are made to forget themselves. Its context makes forgetting God a loss of self-knowledge, sharpening the section's distinction between held and abandoned remembrance. | terra: Those who forgot Allah were made to forget themselves, showing forgetting as both an act of abandonment and a divinely imposed loss of what should be held.

luna: This repeats the pairing in 3:164: the Messenger recites signs, purifies people, and teaches the Book. It directly connects recitation and purification, the two qualities the section brings together through the elevated and purified pages. | terra: The Messenger recites divine signs and teaches the Book among the unlettered, a public continuation of the divinely enabled recitation promised to the Prophet.
terra: Believers are warned not to let wealth and children distract them from Allah's remembrance, specifying worldly attachment as a cause of lost dhikr.
terra: The oath by the pen and what people inscribe foregrounds the material act by which spoken or known content becomes lasting writing.

luna: The section's dictionary form التذكرة is what brings a matter back to mind, and its image asks how the recited word is retained. This verse calls the event a reminder and says a retaining ear “وَتَعِيَهَا أُذُنٌ وَاعِيَةٌ” holds it, joining admonition to attentive preservation. | terra: The event is made a تَذْكِرَة and a receptive ear “retains it” (تَعِيَهَا أُذُنٌ وَاعِيَة); memory is pictured as a vessel that successfully holds what it receives.
terra: The person given his record says هَاؤُمُ اقْرَءُوا كِتَابِيَهْ, another concrete use of reading a collected written account rather than receiving prophetic recitation.

luna: The section's dictionary form القراءة defines reading as joining letters and words in ترتيل. This verse explicitly commands “وَرَتِّلِ الْقُرْآنَ تَرْتِيلًا,” giving that manner of measured recitation a Quranic formulation. | terra: The Prophet is commanded to recite the Quran with تَرْتِيلًا, the same ordered mode in which the source definition says letters and words are joined.
terra: “This is a Reminder” followed by the option to take a path to the Lord presents tadhkira as a practical aid, though it does not name memory loss or pages.
terra: The command to recite whatever is easy of the Quran, repeated within the ayah, explicitly joins recitation to divinely recognized ease.
terra: The passage asks why they turn away from التَّذْكِرَة, establishing rejected reminder as the problem that the opened pages and divine will later clarify.

luna: The section describes written pages as the form that carries a prophetic reminder. In this surah's context of people turning away from the reminder, each person wants to be given “صُحُفًا مُّنَشَّرَةً”; their demand for opened pages contrasts with the reminder already being addressed to them. | terra: Each rejecter demands to be given صُحُفًا مُّنَشَّرَة, separate opened pages, while evading the reminder already before him.
terra: Their demand for pages in 74:52 is diagnosed as a failure to fear the Hereafter, the reverse of the fearing recipient who remembers in 87:10.

luna: The section's dictionary form التذكرة means something used to bring a needed matter back to mind. This verse likewise names the message “تَذْكِرَةٌ,” directly connecting the Quranic reminder to that definition. | terra: The discourse answers the demanded pages by declaring that the existing revelation itself is a تَذْكِرَة.

luna: The section distinguishes the reminder from the person who remembers it. This verse says whoever wills may remember the reminder, making that distinction explicit. | terra: Whoever wills may remember it, naming the act the reminder-pages are meant to produce.

luna: This completes 74:54–55 by saying they do not remember unless God wills. It adds divine will as a limit on the voluntary response, echoing the section's exception in 87:7. | terra: They will not remember unless Allah wills, directly joining recollection to the same divine-will boundary attached to non-forgetting at 87:7.

luna: The section presents 87:6 as Allah causing the Prophet to read. Here the same address restrains his tongue from hurrying to receive the recitation, giving the preservation promise its immediate setting. | terra: The command not to hurry the tongue stages the bodily risk behind the promise of retention: the Prophet need not seize the revelation anxiously before Allah gathers it.

luna: The section's dictionary form قرأت الشيء defines reading as gathering parts together. Here Allah says, “عَلَيْنَا جَمْعَهُ وَقُرْآنَهُ,” making gathering and recitation the divine work behind the promise. | terra: Allah takes responsibility for both جَمْعَهُ, gathering the revelation, and قُرْءَانَهُ, its recitation; this states the section's word-image almost exactly.

luna: The section's dictionary describes reading as joining words in recitation. This verse says that once Allah recites it, the Prophet is to follow that recitation; it spells out how the received words are held. | terra: Once Allah has recited it, the Prophet is to follow its recitation; the verse distinguishes the divine act of giving the gathered reading from the recipient's faithful following.

luna: This follows the collection, recitation, and following in 75:17–18 with “ثُمَّ إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا بَيَانَهُ.” Its contribution is the completing explanation of the recited revelation, not a further claim about memorization. | terra: After gathering and recitation in 75:17-18, Allah also assumes its explanation; this completes the passage's account of the divine custody of the delivered words.
terra: Immediately after the divine gathering and recitation passage, the hearers are said to love the immediate life, continuing directly into the preference diagnosed at 87:16.
terra: The hearers leave the Hereafter while loving the immediate life in 75:20; this supplies the other half of the same near-versus-lasting choice.

luna: The section says people prefer the nearer life. This verse says the people love “الْعَاجِلَةَ” and leave behind a heavy day, giving the same temporal preference in the language of love and neglect. | terra: The rejecters love the immediate life and leave behind a weighty Day, closely repeating the near-life preference and its neglected lasting consequence.

luna: The section names the reminder and the one who remembers it. This verse calls the Quran “تَذْكِرَةٌ” and says whoever wills may take a path to the Lord, spelling out the response to the reminder. | terra: The revelation is a تَذْكِرَة from which whoever wills may take a path to the Lord, presenting reminder as a means for recovering direction.

luna: This follows the choice in 76:29 by saying people do not will unless Allah wills. It adds divine limit to the human choice, resonating with the section's “except what Allah wills.” | terra: Human willing in 76:29 operates only if Allah wills, a close structural parallel to the divine-will qualification on retention in 87:7.
terra: “Everything We have enumerated in a book” presents writing as the form of exhaustive divine collection.

luna: The section contrasts those who remember with those drawn toward the nearer life. This begins the sequence that in 79:38 names the person who prefers worldly life and in 79:39 gives that choice its outcome; its own contribution is the transgression preceding the choice.

luna: The section's dictionary form تُؤْثِرُونَ means giving one thing preference. This verse uses the same root in “وَآثَرَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا,” explicitly describing the person who preferred worldly life. | terra: وَآثَرَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا repeats 87:16's preference for the nearer life almost word for word.

luna: This follows the preference in 79:38 with the Fire as that person's abode. It makes the consequence of preferring the nearer life explicit, alongside the section's warning to those who turn from reminder.

luna: This turns from the person preferring worldly life in 79:38 to the one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains his soul from desire. It gives the counter-choice that illuminates the section's “better and more lasting” Hereafter.
luna: This completes the counter-choice in 79:40 with the Garden as its abode. The result puts the lasting Hereafter opposite the worldly preference described in the section and 79:38.

luna: The section's dictionary form التذكرة is something by which a need is recalled. “إِنَّهَا تَذْكِرَةٌ” calls the revelation itself a reminder, directly connecting the instrument of recall to the scripture. | terra: The revelation is called a تَذْكِرَة, matching the section's reminder as the means by which a needed thing is brought back to mind.

luna: The section distinguishes the reminder from the act of remembering it. “فَمَنْ شَاءَ ذَكَرَهُ” makes that response voluntary, as 87:9–10 distinguishes the reminder from the person who remembers. | terra: فَمَن شَاءَ ذَكَرَهُ makes the reminder something a person may actively retain or recall, moving from the instrument in 80:11 to its use.

luna: The section's dictionary defines suhuf as written sheets and explains that earlier scripture is on such pages. This verse locates the reminder “فِي صُحُفٍ مُكَرَّمَةٍ.” | terra: The reminder of 80:11-12 is located فِي صُحُفٍ مُّكَرَّمَة, explicitly joining recollection to written pages.

luna: The section's page image is writing preserved on sheets. Here the pages are “مَرْفُوعَةٍ مُطَهَّرَةٍ,” adding their elevated and purified status to the reminder carried in them. | terra: The pages are مَرْفُوعَةٍ مُّطَهَّرَة, carrying the surah's height and purification into the physical repository of the reminder.

luna: This continues the pages of 80:13–14 by saying they are in the hands of scribes. The added detail identifies the bearers who write or transmit the page, rather than merely repeating its material form. | terra: The honored pages are in the hands of سفرة, adding agents who carry or write the repository named in 80:13.

luna: This completes the scribe description begun in 80:15: the scribes are noble and righteous. It adds the character of those who handle the pages named in the preceding ayat. | terra: The page-bearers are noble and righteous, completing the scene of an honored, purified, carefully mediated written reminder.

luna: The section says written pages hold what is read and remembered. “وَإِذَا الصُّحُفُ نُشِرَتْ” depicts the scrolls being opened, when their contents become available for reckoning. | terra: When the صُحُف are spread open, pages become disclosed records at judgment; it is the same physical noun in a different repository from prophetic scripture.

luna: The section treats revelation as a reminder. This verse calls the Quran “ذِكْرٌ لِلْعَالَمِينَ,” identifying it as a reminder for all worlds before describing who can choose to respond. | terra: The Quran is a Reminder to the worlds, establishing the object whose reception and willing are qualified in the next two ayat.

luna: This follows 81:27 by saying the reminder is for whoever wills to be upright. It makes the recipient's response explicit, as the section distinguishes between people who remember and avoid the reminder. | terra: The Reminder addresses whoever wills to go straight, specifying the responsive agency of its hearer.

luna: This completes 81:28 with the limit that people do not will unless Allah wills. It echoes the section's exception while keeping the ayah's claim about human willing distinct. | terra: The hearers do not will unless Allah wills, placing response to the Reminder within divine willing as 87:7 does with non-forgetting.
terra: Guardians are set over human beings, introducing preservation as active custody before the scribes are named.
terra: The guardians are “noble writers,” giving the custody of 82:10 a scribal mechanism.
terra: The scribes know what people do, completing the movement from known action to guarded writing.

luna: The section connects remembrance of God's name to prayer and the recited reminder. This verse says that when the Quran is recited to them they do not prostrate, a specific refusal at the meeting of recitation and worship.

luna: The section links the prophet's spoken reminder to written pages. “بَلْ هُوَ قُرْآنٌ مَجِيدٌ” names the Quran as the revelation whose written preservation is specified in the next ayah. | terra: The object being secured is identified as a glorious Quran, keeping recited revelation in view before its written locus is named.

luna: This completes 85:21 by locating that Quran “فِي لَوْحٍ مَحْفُوظٍ.” It gives the section's retained-and-written word an explicit preserved-record counterpart. | terra: The glorious Quran is فِي لَوْحٍ مَّحْفُوظٍ, a written tablet explicitly marked as guarded, the clearest counterpart to retained rather than dropped words.

luna: The section's 87:9 gives the Prophet the command to remind. “فَذَكِّرْ إِنَّمَا أَنْتَ مُذَكِّرٌ” gives the same prophetic stance: remind, while describing him as a reminder. | terra: فَذَكِّرْ إِنَّمَا أَنتَ مُذَكِّرٌ repeats the prophetic stance of 87:9: the Prophet's assigned act is to remind.
luna: This follows the command in 88:21 by saying the Prophet is not a controller over them. It marks the boundary of the reminding role that the section's command leaves unstated.
terra: Allah declares that the Hereafter and الأُولَى belong to Him, setting the same temporal pair against any autonomous preference for the nearer life.
terra: The later state is better than الأُولَى; this reverses preference for the nearer/first condition and uses “first” in a temporal sense beside an enduring better future.

luna: The section's dictionary form أقرأت غيري means causing another to read. Here Allah's command “اقْرَأْ” addresses a human reader directly, a close counterpart to the Prophet being made to recite in 87:6. | terra: The first command اقْرَأْ gives the section's act of gathering letters into recitation as a divine imperative tied to the Lord's name.

luna: The section names reading as the joining of words and 87:6 as causing another to read. The repeated “اقْرَأْ” is likewise a divine command to the Prophet to read, now paired with the Lord's generosity. | terra: The repeated command اقْرَأْ sustains the act of recitation and attributes its possibility to the generous Lord.

luna: The section describes suhuf as material pieces on which writing is made. “الَّذِي عَلَّمَ بِالْقَلَمِ” gives the writing tool behind such pages and connects the recited word to inscription. | terra: The Lord teaches by the pen, supplying the written counterpart to the repeated oral command to read in 96:1 and 96:3.

luna: The section's image moves from words held in memory to words written on pages. “عَلَّمَ الْإِنْسَانَ مَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ” adds the knowledge conveyed and retained through that teaching, though the verse does not itself mention a page. | terra: God teaches the human being what he did not know, completing the movement from divine teaching through pen to received knowledge.

luna: The section says that prophetic books are ذكر and that suhuf are written sheets. This verse brings both together: a Messenger recites “صُحُفًا مُطَهَّرَةً” containing valuable writings. | terra: A messenger from Allah يَتْلُو صُحُفًا مُّطَهَّرَة, bringing oral recitation and purified written pages into a single scene.
terra: The purified pages recited in 98:2 contain upright writings, specifying that the physical leaves hold articulated, authoritative content.

luna: The section quotes the pages' statement that each person's effort will be seen. This verse says whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, making that disclosure concrete at the smallest scale.
luna: This completes 99:7 with the same disclosure for an atom's weight of evil. Its contribution is the other side of the record that reveals each person's deeds.
